thread.title: GameStop Earnings: The New CEO Has Plenty to Do

author: David Marino-Nachison
title: GameStop Earnings: The New CEO Has Plenty to Do
text:
Photo: Getty Images Michael Mauler has some work to do. 
Mauler, named CEO of GameStop (GME) in February—a move that coincided with a few other high-level defections—was previously its executive vice president and president of international. (Its previous CEO, Paul Raines, who had battled cancer, died in March at 53.) He now runs a company that has seen its shares substantially underperform the S&P 500 in 2018. 
Not all the news out of the Barron’s Next 50 stock has been downbeat. In January, GameStop turned in a holiday report—covering the 9 weeks ended Dec. 30—in which sales rose more than 10% on a same-store sales boost of nearly 12%. New game hardware sales, driven by Nintendo’s popular Switch , were up 38%. 
But there were questions, too. GameStop’s “Technology Brands” business, which sells mobile phones and service, among other things—it represents about 10% of sales, but with a high gross margin—fell nearly 19% during the holiday season. (The company blamed that in part on limited supply of Apple’s (AAPL) iPhone X.) 
And at a time when videogame sales are increasingly digital, GameStop turned in digital holiday revenues under 5%; high-margin used videogame sales fell, as they had all year. 
The company is scheduled to report fourth-quarter financial results Wednesday after the market’s close. The company has guided investors toward quarterly EPS somewhere between $1.78 and $2.08; Wall Street is looking for $1.99, according to FactSet. 
Mauler clearly has plenty on his plate. “GameStop faces another pivotal year in FY18 to either prove its skeptics wrong or start down a fairly steep slippery slope,” Ascendiant Capital wrote in January. 
On Monday, Wedbush analysts—who have a $22.50 price target on the stock, some 60% above current levels—were optimistic that buybacks could boost earnings but worried about big-picture issues with the videogames business and Technology Brands. Those issues, they wrote, make the shares “difficult to value.”
